Right: the 3-core, the part in which every node keeps at least three neighbors, is the cluster A, B, C, D in the accent color; E to H and their edges are peeled away and drawn dashed." width="100%"} The k-core is the maximal subgraph where all nodes have degree >= k. Iteratively removes nodes with degree < k until all remaining nodes satisfy the condition. Removing a node lowers the degree of its neighbors, which can push them below `k` in turn, so peeling continues until nothing more changes. What remains is the densely interconnected heart of the network, stripped of its periphery. The k-cores are nested: the `(k+1)`-core is always contained in the k-core. The k-core is useful for: - finding the cohesive core of a social, collaboration, or protein interaction network - removing low-degree noise (pendant nodes, chains, sparse fringes) before analysis or visualization - identifying influential spreaders, which tend to sit in the innermost cores To get the core number of every node in one pass instead of extracting one core at a time, use `coreness()`; related extractions are `k_shell()` (coreness exactly `k`), `k_crust()` (coreness at most `k`), and `k_truss()` (an edge-based analogue). Degrees count edges without weights. For directed graphs, degree means out-degree. The original graph is not modified. The returned graph keeps the node and edge IDs, labels, weights and attributes of the original. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [k]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Minimum degree required for nodes to remain in the k-core. Must be a non-negative integer. `k=0` keeps the whole graph, `k=1` drops isolated nodes, and `k=2` removes all trees hanging off the graph (pendant nodes and chains), leaving only nodes on or between cycles. A `k` larger than the graph's maximum coreness returns an empty graph. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : New graph containing only the k-core nodes and the edges between them. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} The graph below has a dense cluster (A, B, C, D, every pair connected), a loop E-F-G attached to it, and a pendant node H. The 2-core peels away only H. For the 3-core, F has only two neighbors and G drops to two once H is gone; removing them leaves E with just C and D, so E goes too and only the cluster survives: ::: {#99c851ff .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ( ec.Graph() .add_nodes(["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F", "G", "H"]) .add_edges([("A", "B"), ("A", "C"), ("A", "D"), ("B", "C"), ("B", "D"), ("C", "D"), ("C", "E"), ("D", "E"), ("E", "F"), ("F", "G"), ("G", "D"), ("G", "H")]) ) core_2 = graph.k_core(2) core_3 = graph.k_core(3) { "2-core": sorted(core_2.get_node_df()["label"].to_list()), "3-core": sorted(core_3.get_node_df()["label"].to_list()), } ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` {'2-core': ['A', 'B', 'C', 'D', 'E', 'F', 'G'], '3-core': ['A', 'B', 'C', 'D']} ``` ::: ::: The core is an ordinary graph and can be analyzed further. The 3-core here is a complete graph on four nodes, so it has all six possible edges and a density of `1.0`: ::: {#9be163bc .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} (core_3.count_edges(), core_3.density()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` (6, 1.0) ``` ::: ::: A path graph has no cycles, so repeatedly removing its endpoints eventually removes everything and its 2-core is empty: ::: {#e4f07c9b .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} ec.Graph().add_path_graph(6).k_core(2).count_nodes() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` 0 ``` ::: :::
